A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPARC and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and extensive appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-alignment, probing, segmentation, retrieval, and ablation results on Open Images and MS-COCO, plus qualitative appendix analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated USAE comparisons, label-purity measurements, reconstruction matrices, runtime measurements, and localization failure cases.

M1.justification: The stream-specific affine encoders and decoders, aggregated-logit Global TopK selection, ReLU, reconstruction objectives, and auxiliary dead-neuron handling remain unchanged. v2 clarifies why streams retain separate activation magnitudes and condenses the loss equations without establishing a different SPARC procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use Open Images and MS-COCO for the same image/text representation, attribution, segmentation, and retrieval tasks, including external-query examples. The additional encoder combinations change model configurations, while label purity and background-localization examples extend evaluation within existing coverage.

E2.justification: USAE changes from a discussed prior method in v1 to an evaluated comparator for activation consistency, concept alignment, probing, and segmentation, as well as the new purity and reconstruction comparisons. Existing Local TopK, DETR, and CLIP comparisons are retained. This substantially expands direct comparison with the principal competing method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces purity evaluation using top-10, 25, 50, 100, and all examples, variance-weighted R² reconstruction evaluation, and encoder combinations containing up to ten streams. Reported Jaccard evaluation narrows from taxonomy depths 0–5 to depth 5. Existing SPARC training budgets, splits, probe procedures, and downstream evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis across purity subset sizes and encoder compositions, and extends localization failure analysis with scene-object, facial-feature, and background queries in Figures 26–30. The taxonomy-depth sensitivity analysis is removed. Original latent-count, sparsity, cross-loss, and learning-rate sweeps remain, with the latter two moved to Appendix B.

E5.justification: v2 adds standard errors over latents for Jaccard alignment and label purity, and over tasks for probe losses. v1 reports these retained alignment and probe results without uncertainty. The fixed training seed and task-specific split seeds remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: USAE Jaccard is 0.2166 versus the retained SPARC value of 0.8018, and new purity and reconstruction tables provide direct comparisons across configurations. The new matrices include unfavorable SPARC outcomes, such as negative Swin reconstruction R² in Table 10. Original segmentation and retrieval scores remain; the Global-plus-cross CLIP-image probe loss changes from 0.5355 to 0.5354, and depth-0–4 Jaccard entries disappear.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds an asymptotic derivation: with fixed batch size and comparable feature dimensions, SPARC costs O(M²Ld) per batch versus USAE's O(MLd). The central model mathematics remains equivalent, although v1's explicit NMSE definition is omitted. The added standard R² formula does not constitute a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that Global TopK and cross-reconstruction create aligned sparse concepts across models and modalities, achieve approximately 0.80 Jaccard alignment, and enable localization and retrieval. v2's explicit USAE comparison supplies new evidence for the retained superiority claim without changing the central contributions or claimed capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 expands interpretation through reconstruction-direction asymmetry, reasons for retaining separate stream activations, and qualifications on label purity as an interpretability proxy. Appendix F.3 identifies foreground bias and failures on background queries beyond v1's detailed-part example. Computational-cost caveats and a new Broader Impact discussion further expand applicability and misuse considerations; the taxonomy-depth interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: New Appendices A.4–A.5 document cached-feature training, H100 runtimes, the USAE implementation, matched hyperparameters, and USAE-specific settings. Appendix C specifies additional encoder checkpoints, feature extraction, and preprocessing. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. The code link remains unchanged, while the explicit NMSE normalization formula is lost.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of BatchTopK and citations for the additional encoders and R². The central positioning against USAE and earlier concept-alignment approaches remains substantially unchanged. The Burns reference's update from preprint to conference publication identifies the same work rather than a new citation.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses the introduction and training-objective explanation, rewrites concept-alignment exposition, and reorganizes the empirical narrative. Retrieval moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix G, while cross-loss and learning-rate subsections move to Appendix B. These are meaningful structural and explanatory revisions beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds purity and reconstruction tables, an encoder inventory, and five failure-case figures. Existing comparison tables gain method columns, USAE rows, or uncertainty formatting; the Jaccard table replaces hierarchy-depth columns with a single depth-5 summary. Retrieval displays and two ablation plots move to appendices, while original qualitative images and ablation plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 criticizes USAE without directly evaluating it. v2 resolves this central evidential gap through documented, matched-budget comparisons, while broader reconstruction tests, uncertainty reporting, and explicit failure cases strengthen credibility and applicability assessment. Reproducibility documentation also improves substantially. Losing coarser-depth alignment results and the explicit NMSE definition reduces some detail, and the new reconstruction results do not support uniform superiority, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
